idiom_name: Proxy(target, handler) typed via ProxyHandler<T> / generic factory (+ mapped types)
implementation_notes: The runtime mechanism is JavaScript's built-in Proxy with traps; TypeScript's contribution is keeping the substitution honest at compile time: write a generic factory such as `function proxied<T extends object>(target: T, handler: ProxyHandler<T>): T` so call sites still see T, type trap parameters against keyof T, and reach for mapped/utility types (Readonly<T>, Partial<T>) when the 'proxy' is purely a compile-time interface change. A hand-written forwarding class that implements the interface and delegates each member is still the honest choice when a real nominal type is needed, when no runtime handler overhead is acceptable, or when targeting runtimes without the Proxy API.
pitfalls: TypeScript assumes new Proxy returns the target's type; a trap that returns something incompatible still type-checks, so the compiler cannot verify the proxy's contract.
Proxy invariants are enforced at runtime (non-configurable/non-writable target properties), and private #fields and internal slots break because the receiver is the proxy.
Readonly<T>/as const only stop writes at compile time; if runtime enforcement is required, that is a Proxy or Object.freeze - do not conflate the two.
Typed traps often need casts (prop as keyof T); keep the casts inside the factory so the unsoundness is localized and call sites stay fully checked.
